content: A nanometre, equivalent to 1 × 10⁻⁹ metres, is a unit of length often used to describe the sizes of atoms, the lengths of chemical bonds, the wavelengths of visible light spectra, and the dimensions of components in integrated circuits. It is also widely applied in structural biology. The ångström, a related unit, is named after Anders Jonas Ångström, a Swedish physicist. Unicode includes the ångström sign at U+212B (Å), but this is normalized to U+00C5 (Å), which is considered the correct representation. It is recommended to use U+00C5 directly to avoid encoding errors. The ångström is named after Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874), a Swedish physicist and one of the pioneers of spectroscopy. Ångström is also known for his contributions to astrophysics, heat transfer, terrestrial magnetism, and studies of the aurora borealis. In 1868, he created a spectrum chart of solar radiation, expressing the wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation in multiples of one ten-millionth of a millimetre (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ metres). This unit of length later became known as the ångström (Å). The human eye is sensitive to wavelengths ranging from approximately 4,000 ångströms (violet) to 7,000 ångströms (deep red). The ångström provided a convenient unit for describing these wavelengths without resorting to fractional units. Due to its proximity to the scale of atomic and molecular structures, the ångström also became widely used in chemistry and crystallography. Although originally intended to correspond to 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ metres, the ångström required more precise definition for spectral analysis than the metre, which, until 1960, was still defined based on the length of a metal bar stored in Paris. In 1927, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures endorsed a definition of the ångström based on the wavelength of light emitted by a specific transition in krypton-86, equating it to 4,696.1 international ångströms. From 1927 to 1960, the ångström was a secondary unit of length used in spectroscopy, defined independently of the metre. However, in 1960, the metre was redefined in terms of the wavelength of light, aligning the ångström as a submultiple of the metre. Today, the ångström is defined as exactly 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ metres. Consequently, there are 10,000 ångströms in a micrometre (commonly called a micron, abbreviated as μm, with 1 million microns in a metre) and 10 ångströms in a nanometre (1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ metres). Despite its historical significance, the ångström is now less commonly used, with the nanometre (nm) being the preferred unit. The ångström is officially discouraged by both the International Committee for Weights and Measures and the American National Standard for Metric Practice.
